OSCP exam — hands-on and report format?
column2: A 24-hour proctored hacking window, then a separate ~24-hour window to write and submit a professional PDF report.

#separator:: OSCP total points and pass mark?
column2: 100 points total; 70 needed to pass.

#separator:: How are the OSCP+ 100 points distributed?
column2: One Active Directory set of 3 machines = 40 points; 3 standalone machines = 60 points (20 each) — verify machine counts and weighting on OffSec.

#separator:: Are there bonus points on the OSCP exam?
column2: No — bonus points were removed as of 1 November 2024; the score is exam performance only.

#separator:: local.txt vs proof.txt?
column2: local.txt proves low-privilege/initial foothold access; proof.txt proves full privilege escalation (admin/root).

#separator:: Can you pass the hacking and still fail OSCP?
column2: Yes — the report is a graded deliverable; insufficient documentation can fail an otherwise-passing exam.

#separator:: What does OffSec's 'Try Harder' philosophy emphasise?
column2: Self-reliance and a repeatable methodology over hand-holding and memorization; public exploits often need modification.

#separator:: CEH vs OSCP in one line?
column2: CEH is knowledge-based (mostly multiple choice); OSCP is hands-on — you must actually exploit live machines and report it.

#separator:: What is the master skill of OSCP?
column2: Enumeration — most failed attempts trace to missed information, not missing exploits.

#separator:: Enumeration workflow order?
column2: Host discovery → port scan → service/version detection → per-service deep dive.

#separator:: Passive vs active reconnaissance?
column2: Passive sends no packets to the target (third-party data, invisible); active probes the target directly and appears in its logs.

#separator:: Why must you scan UDP, not just TCP?
column2: UDP is slow and easy to forget, but SNMP lives on UDP 161 — skipping UDP is a classic OSCP mistake.

#separator:: Why is a service version string so valuable?
column2: It points to known weaknesses and the right enumeration follow-up.

#separator:: What can SMB (TCP 445) enumeration reveal?
column2: Shares, share permissions, users, groups and OS/version; anonymous/guest access can leak files or a user list.

#separator:: What can SNMP leak when default community strings survive?
column2: Via the MIB: interfaces, routing tables, running processes, installed software and user accounts.

#separator:: Default community strings SNMP tools try?
column2: public and private.

#separator:: What should you do after gaining each foothold?
column2: Re-enumerate from scratch — each new host is a fresh vantage point that may expose internal-only services.

#separator:: Nmap vs the Nmap Scripting Engine (NSE)?
column2: Nmap does discovery/port/version scanning; NSE runs pluggable scripts that automate service-specific enumeration.

#separator:: Most common OSCP initial-access surface?
column2: Web applications (HTTP/HTTPS).

#separator:: Root cause common to most web flaws?
column2: Trusting user-controlled input — it changes the meaning of a query, path or command.

#separator:: SQL injection — target and defence?
column2: Targets the database query layer; defend with parameterized queries/prepared statements and least-privilege DB accounts.

#separator:: LFI vs RFI?
column2: Local File Inclusion loads files already on the server; Remote File Inclusion loads an attacker-controlled URL, which can lead to code execution.

#separator:: Defence against file inclusion?
column2: Never build include paths from user input; use a fixed allow-list of permitted files; disable remote includes in the runtime.

#separator:: Unrestricted file upload — why it works?
column2: The app accepts an executable file type and stores it in a web-accessible executable location, so it can be requested to run code.

#separator:: Defence against unrestricted file upload?
column2: Allow-list file types, validate content (not just extension), store outside the web root, serve as non-executable.

#separator:: Command injection — target and defence?
column2: Targets code that passes input into an OS shell; defend by avoiding shelling out, using argument arrays, and validating input.

#separator:: Directory traversal vs LFI?
column2: Traversal (../) typically reads arbitrary files outside the intended directory; inclusion can lead to execution of the included file.

#separator:: Defence against authentication/access bypass?
column2: Enforce authentication and authorization server-side on every request, use strong session management, deny by default.

#separator:: Burp Suite — purpose?
column2: An intercepting proxy to inspect and (with authorization) modify HTTP requests/responses — the core web-testing workbench.

#separator:: Brute force vs dictionary attack?
column2: Brute force tries every combination in a keyspace; a dictionary attack tries a curated wordlist of likely passwords — far faster.

#separator:: Password spraying?
column2: Trying one common password across many accounts, staying below the per-account lockout threshold — a common AD technique.

#separator:: Why does offline hash cracking sidestep lockout?
column2: The target service is never touched, so account lockout and rate limits do not apply — cracking is unlimited and silent.

#separator:: What slows offline hash cracking?
column2: A slow, salted hash algorithm and a long, strong password.

#separator:: Why does length beat complexity?
column2: Each added character multiplies the search space far more than swapping a letter for a symbol; a long passphrase outlasts a short complex one.

#separator:: Client-side attack concept?
column2: Targets the user's software (browser, document reader) — e.g. a malicious document whose macro runs attacker actions if the user enables active content.

#separator:: Single highest-impact defence against password attacks?
column2: Multi-factor authentication — a guessed or cracked password alone is insufficient.

#separator:: Hydra vs John the Ripper vs Hashcat?
column2: Hydra drives online login guessing across protocols; John cracks hashes offline (many formats); Hashcat is a GPU-accelerated offline cracker.

#separator:: Exam habit: what do you do with any credentials you find?
column2: Reuse them — a password recovered on one host often unlocks another; always test discovered creds elsewhere.

#separator:: Is privilege escalation exploit-driven or enumeration-driven?
column2: Enumeration-driven — you inventory the host and find misconfigured trust, rather than memorizing exploits.

#separator:: What does escalation almost always exploit?
column2: Misplaced trust — a privileged process, file or schedule that an unprivileged user can influence.

#separator:: Linux escalation classes to check?
column2: sudo rules, SUID/SGID binaries, weak file/dir permissions, service/PATH misconfig, credentials in files, cron/scheduled jobs, kernel/capabilities.

#separator:: Why do SUID/SGID binaries escalate?
column2: They run as their owner (often root) regardless of caller; one with a shell escape or relative-path trust runs your code as root.

#separator:: How does a sudo rule lead to root?
column2: A permitted command that can spawn a shell, read arbitrary files, or run a script you control hands over the target's privileges.

#separator:: How does a writable cron/service PATH escalate?
column2: A root job or service running a writable script — or a planted binary earlier in PATH — executes your content with its privileges.

#separator:: Windows escalation classes to check?
column2: Service misconfigurations, weak file/registry permissions, token/privilege abuse, stored credentials, scheduled tasks, always-elevated installers, missing patches.

#separator:: Why does a service misconfiguration escalate on Windows?
column2: A service running as SYSTEM that launches an attacker-controlled binary (weak ACL or unquoted path) executes it as SYSTEM.

#separator:: Unifying defence against all privilege escalation?
column2: Least privilege and PAM — remove excess privilege/trust, keep no standing secrets on hosts, and detect via EDR and session recording.

#separator:: How does LAPS help against Windows escalation/lateral movement?
column2: It gives each host a unique local-admin password so one cracked password does not unlock every machine.

#separator:: OSCP AD attack chain order?
column2: Enumeration → credential attacks → lateral movement → domain compromise.

#separator:: Why is AD enumeration so productive?
column2: AD is readable by any authenticated user by design; misconfigured ACLs and over-privileged groups reveal escalation paths.

#separator:: Pass-the-Hash — what trust does it abuse?
column2: NTLM accepting a password's hash in place of the plaintext, so a recovered hash authenticates without the password.

#separator:: Pass-the-Ticket — what does it abuse?
column2: Kerberos ticket replay — a stolen ticket is reused to access services as the victim until it expires.

#separator:: Kerberoasting — what it needs and abuses?
column2: Any authenticated user requests a service ticket for an account with an SPN; the ticket is encrypted with the service key, so a weak service password can be cracked offline.

#separator:: Best defence against Kerberoasting?
column2: Strong, long, managed service-account passwords (gMSA); minimal SPN exposure; PAM rotation; alert on abnormal service-ticket volumes.

#separator:: Defence against Pass-the-Hash?
column2: Reduce/disable legacy NTLM, Credential Guard, LAPS, tiering so a workstation hash cannot reach Tier 0, and PAM so admins never type reusable passwords on endpoints.

#separator:: What is the attacker's fuel in an AD chain?
column2: Standing, reusable privileged credentials on endpoints — PAM brokers and rotates them, breaking the chain.

#separator:: How does tiered administration limit lateral movement?
column2: Separate admin tiers stop workstation credentials from reaching servers and domain controllers.

#separator:: What is domain compromise?
column2: Reaching a Domain Admin account or the Domain Controller and asserting control over the directory.

#separator:: Pivoting vs port forwarding vs tunneling?
column2: Pivoting uses a foothold as a relay into unreachable segments; port forwarding maps one internal service through it; tunneling wraps traffic (often in SSH) to route many connections.

#separator:: Local vs remote vs dynamic forwarding?
column2: Local exposes a remote internal service on a local port; remote exposes your local service to the internal network; dynamic turns the foothold into a SOCKS-style proxy.

#separator:: When do you know you need to pivot?
column2: When the foothold can reach a target that scanning from your own machine cannot.

#separator:: How does network segmentation stop pivoting?
column2: A compromised zone cannot freely reach others, so the pivot has far fewer reachable targets; microsegmentation denies lateral flows by default.

#separator:: Pivot vs jump host — same shape, opposite intent?
column2: A pivot is unsanctioned and hidden using stolen access; a bastion/jump host is sanctioned and mandatory, removing direct paths and recording every session.

#separator:: First step before forwarding anything through a foothold?
column2: Map the foothold's networks — its interfaces, reachable subnets and internal hosts.

#separator:: Note-taking discipline in the exam?
column2: Capture commands, outputs and screenshots (host identity and current user) as you go — a flag value without documented method earns no points.
